claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater high-temperature plastic strain than commercially used pure tungsten.
Equimolar WTaTiVZr has greater high-temperature toughness than commercially used pure tungsten.
Severe lattice distortion caused by multielement mixing governs the enhanced plastic strain and toughness.
Lattice distortion in WTaTiVZr lowers the effective Peierls barrier for dislocation glide.
A homogeneous, refined microstructure delays crack initiation under plasma-facing conditions.
The proposed alloy is equimolar WTaTiVZr.
As-processed WTaTiVZr has a random solid-solution microstructure.
As-processed WTaTiVZr contains minimal secondary-phase precipitation.
Severe lattice distortion induces a refined grain structure and homogeneous dislocation substructure.
Multielement alloying reduces the energy barriers for dislocation nucleation and glide in WTaTiVZr.
Reduced dislocation barriers enhance thermally activated dislocation mobility and dynamic recovery.
Enhanced dislocation mobility changes the response from brittle and strain-localized in pure tungsten to ductile and spatially distributed in WTaTiVZr.
Distributed plastic deformation delays crack initiation and growth.
At high temperature, WTaTiVZr will have lower yield stress than pure tungsten.
At high temperature, WTaTiVZr will sustain greater plastic strain before failure than pure tungsten.
At high temperature, WTaTiVZr will absorb more mechanical energy before failure than pure tungsten.
Pure tungsten has a high Peierls barrier that limits its plastic strain and toughness under the proposed conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies only in a temperature window where thermal activation assists dislocation motion without excessive grain growth or oxidation.
The proposed mechanism presumes a uniform, single-phase solid solution without deleterious segregation.
Irradiation and long-term thermal exposure may alter the operative deformation mechanisms.
